Heading that opens Section 1, Introduction; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

The overview motivates the specification. It says establishing the provenance of media is critical to trust, because mis-attributed and mis-contextualised content spreads quickly on social platforms and inauthentic content is rising, and because creators cannot currently attach metadata to their work in a secure, tamper-evident and standardised way across platforms. Provenance lets creators and editors disclose how an asset was created and changed; each change is added while the existing provenance is preserved. The C2PA developed the specification to enable global, opt-in adoption of digital provenance, informed by requirements from industry experts and partners including the Project Origin Alliance and the Content Authenticity Initiative, and notes that regulators could also use it to establish standards.

The scope: the specification describes the technical side of the C2PA architecture, a model for storing and accessing cryptographically verifiable information whose trustworthiness is assessed against a defined trust model, including how to create and process a C2PA Manifest and how digital signatures provide tamper-evidence and trust. It was written after the C2PA's Guiding Principles, which focus on privacy and personal control of data and on potential abuse; implementers are strongly encouraged to let creators and publishers control whether certain provenance data is included. Quoting those principles, it says C2PA specifications do not judge provenance data as good or bad, only whether its assertions validate as bound to the asset, well-formed and untampered. The specification should not harm content accessibility, and other C2PA documents cover user experience and threat and harms modelling.

The technical overview: C2PA information is a series of statements, called assertions, about matters such as asset creation, edit actions, capture device details and bindings to content; together they make up an asset's provenance and act as trust signals for a human. Assertions are wrapped with further information into a claim, which the claim generator signs on behalf of the signer with the signer's credential, producing the claim signature. A claim generator (hardware or software) binds the assertions, claim and claim signature into a verifiable unit, the C2PA Manifest (Figure 1), and the set of C2PA Manifests stored in the asset's Content Credential is its provenance data.

Trust in C2PA rests on the identity of the signer associated with the key used to sign a claim, per the specification's trust model. Combined with trusted time stamps, claim signatures can be validated indefinitely to determine whether a claim was signed while the signing credentials were valid and not revoked.

A worked example: a C2PA-enabled camera or phone takes a photograph and creates a manifest whose assertions include details about the camera, a thumbnail and cryptographic hashes binding the photograph to the manifest. The assertions are listed in a claim, which is digitally signed, and the whole C2PA Manifest (Figure 2) is embedded in the output JPEG, where it remains valid indefinitely. A manifest consumer such as a validator then validates the signature and its credential, checks each assertion, and presents the information and signature so the user can make an informed decision about the content's trustworthiness.

The design goals, listed in Table 1 so the technology works across hardware and software worldwide and is accessible to all: privacy (users control their information), responsibility (consumers can determine provenance), scalability (web-scale creation and validation), extensibility (others can add metadata and credentials without C2PA approval), interoperability, whole-workflow applicability (provenance kept from creation through publication), technology minimalism (rely on well-established techniques), security (trustworthy integrity and source, with expert review), content ubiquity (all common media types, including documents), flexible locality (online and offline), global universality, accessibility (e.g. WCAG), harms and misuse (avert harms, including to human rights and vulnerable groups), and evolving (continual review against these goals).

Reading guidance: the specification is easier to read in the parts relevant to one's role, in a useful order, than from start to finish. It lists three roles, each with its own section: claim generators (1.5), validators (1.6) and security reviewers (1.7).

A reading path for claim generators, whose core flow is to create assertions, reference them from a claim, include relevant ingredients, bind the claim to the asset, sign it, and package everything as a valid C2PA Manifest; examples are cameras, recorders, AI asset creators, editing software and transcoders. Required reading, each with its reason: the Technical Overview; selected Glossary terms; Assertions; Unique Identifiers (C2PA URNs); Binding to Content (hard bindings, and soft bindings such as watermarks for recovering a stripped manifest); Claims; URI References; Manifests; Embedding C2PA Manifests (only the supported formats); the standard assertions the generator emits; Cryptography; and parts of the Trust Model. Live Media is required only for live content, and Validation only for generators that support ingredients, since ingredients must be validated on ingestion — though any generator can use it as a QA checklist.

A reading path for validators, whose core flow is to locate the C2PA Manifest Store, identify the active manifest, validate the claim and signature, check signer trust and credential status, validate assertions, ingredients and the content binding, and return or display the results; examples are photo galleries, social media platforms, news publishers and verification tools. Required reading: the Technical Overview; selected Glossary terms; parts of Manifests; hard and soft bindings; hashing and signatures in Cryptography; parts of the Trust Model (validation states, trust lists, X.509 certificates); all of Validation, the core validator section; and the standard assertions the product handles. User Experience is needed only when results are shown to users, so as not to mislead them, and Live Media only for live content. Embedding, Assertions, Claims and URI References are listed as helpful context on the data structures.

A reading path for security reviewers, who check whether the trust model, cryptographic algorithms, validation process and security guidance meet current best practice. Required reading: the Design Goals (including what the specification is and is not meant to prove), the Technical Overview, Information Security Considerations (the core section, on threats, harms, misuse and abuse), the Trust Model, Cryptography and Validation. Helpful context: Assertions, Binding to Content (including the risks when assets are modified, stripped or matched by soft binding), Claims, Manifests (integrity, ambiguity, stripping and substitution risks), the relevant embedding formats, and the standard assertions relevant to the reviewer's threat model. User Experience is needed when reviewing user-facing trust signals, since misleading presentation can undermine security claims, and Live Media when reviewing live workflows.
Heading that opens Section 2, Glossary; the block holds no text beyond the heading.
Heading for Section 2.1, Introductory terms; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

Defines an actor as a human or non-human (hardware or software) participant in the C2PA ecosystem, such as a camera, image editing software, a cloud service or the person using them. A note adds that an organisation or group of actors may also count as an actor.

Defines the claim generator as the non-human (hardware or software) actor that generates the claim about an asset and the claim signature, leading to the asset's C2PA Manifest. A note says it is a component of a larger system, such as a library, SDK or shared service that a signer relies on, and is not the signer, so it does not take responsibility for the content of the claim or its assertions.
Defines the signer as the holder of the credential whose private key is used to sign the claim; the signer is identified by the subject of that credential.
Defines a manifest consumer as an actor that consumes an asset with an associated C2PA Manifest in order to obtain the provenance data from that manifest.
Defines a validator as a manifest consumer whose role is to perform the actions described in the specification's validation section.
Defines an action as an operation performed by an actor on an asset, with examples "create", "embed" and "apply filter".
Heading for Section 2.2, Assets and Content; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

Defines digital content as the part of an asset that is the actual content, such as an image's pixels, together with any technical metadata needed to understand it, such as a colour profile or encoding parameters.
Defines asset metadata as non-technical information about an asset and its digital content.

Defines an asset as a file or stream of data containing digital content, asset metadata and, optionally, a C2PA Manifest. A note extends "file" here to include cloud-native and dynamically generated data.
Defines a derived asset as one created from an existing asset by performing actions that modify its digital content, for example a shortened audio stream or a document with added pages.

Defines an asset rendition as a representation of an asset, either part of it or a wholly new asset, whose digital content has undergone a non-editorial transformation such as re-encoding or scaling; the example is a video re-encoded for a lower screen resolution or bandwidth.

Defines a composed asset as one built from a collection of parts or fragments of digital content, called ingredients, taken from one or more other assets. When it starts from an existing asset it is a special case of a derived asset, but it can also start from a blank slate. Examples are a video assembled from imported clips and audio segments, and an image with another image superimposed on it.

Defines an editorial transformation as one that alters the intent or the meaning (or both) of the digital content. A note says every editorial transformation is perceptible, but not every perceptible transformation is editorial.
Defines a perceptible transformation as one that alters how humans perceive the digital content under normal conditions.
Heading for Section 2.3, Core Aspects of C2PA; the block holds no text beyond the heading.
Defines an assertion as a data structure representing a statement about the asset, either made by the signer or simply gathered when the claim is generated; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.

Defines the assertion store as the logical collection of assertions that a claim references within a C2PA Manifest, stored together as one construct, and points to the Assertion Store section for its full structure.

Defines a claim as a digitally signed, tamper-evident data structure that references a set of assertions about an asset and the information needed to represent the content binding, and that declares any redacted assertions; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.
Defines the claim signature as the digital signature on the claim, made with the private key owned by a signer; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.

Defines a C2PA Manifest as the set of provenance information about an asset formed by one or more assertions (including content bindings), a single claim and a claim signature; it is part of a C2PA Manifest Store. A note says a manifest can reference other manifests.
Defines a C2PA Manifest Store as a collection of C2PA Manifests that can be embedded in an asset or kept external to it.

Defines Content Credential as the preferred non-technical term for a C2PA Manifest, so an asset's manifest store represents its Content Credentials. The term also names the C2PA technology as a whole and is treated as a plural noun: one manifest is a Content Credential, while several manifests or the broader concept are Content Credentials.
Defines the active manifest as the last manifest in a C2PA Manifest Store's list, the one whose content bindings can be validated, and points to the Manifest Store section for its full structure.
Defines provenance as the logical concept of understanding an asset's history and its interactions with actors and other assets, as represented by the provenance data.

Defines provenance data as the set of C2PA Manifests for an asset and, for a composed asset, for its ingredients, and points to the Manifests section for its full structure. A note says a manifest can reference other manifests.

Defines authenticity as a property of digital content comprising a set of facts, such as the provenance data and hard bindings, that can be cryptographically verified as not having been tampered with.

Defines content binding as information that associates digital content to a specific C2PA Manifest associated with a specific asset, either as a hard binding or a soft binding; the full structural description is in the Binding to Content section.
Defines a hard binding as one or more cryptographic hashes that uniquely identify either the entire asset or a portion of it.
Defines a soft binding as a content identifier that is either not statistically unique, such as a fingerprint, or embedded as an invisible watermark in the identified digital content.

Defines trust signals as the collection of information that can inform a Manifest Consumer's judgment of the trustworthiness of an asset, in addition to the signer on which the fundamental trust model relies.
Defines the C2PA Trust List as a C2PA-managed list of X.509 certificate trust anchors that issue certificates to hardware and software signers, who use them to sign claims.
Defines the C2PA TSA Trust List as a C2PA-managed list of X.509 certificate trust anchors that issue certificates to Time Stamping Authorities (TSAs).
Heading that opens section 2.4 Additional Terms; it carries no text of its own.
Defines a Durable Content Credential as a Content Credential for which one or more soft bindings exist that enable its discovery in a manifest repository.

Defines a fingerprint as a set of inherent properties computable from digital content that identifies the content or near duplicates of it. An example notes that if an asset becomes separated from its C2PA Manifest through removal or corruption of its metadata, a fingerprint of its digital content could be used to search a database and recover the asset with an intact C2PA Manifest.

Defines an invisible watermark as information incorporated in a substantially human-imperceptible way into the digital content of an asset, which can be used, for example, to uniquely identify the asset or to store a reference to a C2PA Manifest.
Defines a visible watermark as a perceptible component of the digital content carrying some human-consumable information about the provenance of the asset.
Defines a manifest repository as a repository into which C2PA Manifests and C2PA Manifest Stores can be placed, and which can be searched using a content binding.
Presents Figure 3, a diagram showing how the various elements of a Content Credential come together to represent the C2PA architecture.

Specifies that the key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14, RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 when they appear in any casing. States that CDDL rules and type definitions in the C2PA CDDL schemas are normative while comments within them are non-normative, and that schema validation is neither necessary nor recommended. If the CDDL schema conflicts with the normative text of the specification, the normative text takes precedence.
Heading that opens section 5 Versioning; it carries no text of its own.

Describes how constructs such as box labels, assertions, claims and time stamps have evolved, and defines a deprecated construct as one that a claim generator shall not write but that a validator should read. Recommends that a claim generator declare the specification version it used by providing a specVersion key in the claim_generator_info field, which declares that the active manifest was produced per that version and contains no constructs deprecated in it. Requires a validator to be compatible with at least one specification version and to support all non-deprecated constructs of any version it is compatible with, while allowing it to ignore constructs it does not support (deprecated or unknown) and process the rest of the C2PA Manifest. Also recommends that a claim generator performing ingredient validation add a specVersion key to the validation-results-map to declare the version used for the validation procedure.

Describes the C2PA aim that Content Credentials created under newer specification versions remain parseable and validatable by implementations of earlier versions wherever practical. Recommends that implementations gracefully handle unknown or unrecognized data without fatal errors, preserve the integrity of a C2PA Manifest even when parts of it cannot be fully interpreted, and indicate partial interpretation to users or downstream systems rather than rejecting the manifest outright. Notes that breaking changes may occasionally be necessary for significant advances or fundamental security, trust or interoperability concerns, in which case versioning guidance and migration considerations will be explicitly documented.
Points to the Version History appendix for a detailed version history of the specification.
Heading that opens section 6 Normative References; it carries no text of its own.
Lists the core formats referenced normatively: CBOR, JSON, JSON-LD, the HTML Living Standard, and the JPEG universal metadata box format (JUMBF).
Lists the schema references: CDDL, JSON Schema (2020-12), and the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative.

Lists the normative references for digital and electronic signatures, including CMS, the data URL scheme, the Base16/Base32/Base64 encodings, the X.509 PKI Time-Stamp Protocol, OCSP, PKCS #1, JSON Pointer, and several X.509 algorithm-identifier and logotype RFCs. It also lists the COSE structures, initial algorithms, RSA and X.509 header parameter specifications, CBOR Web Tokens, the ML-DSA references including FIPS 204, and ETSI documents on JAdES, AdES signature creation and validation (ETSI EN 319 102-1), and trusted lists (ETSI TS 119 602 and TS 119 612).

Lists the embeddable formats referenced normatively, including ISO BMFF, PDF 1.7 and 2.0, JPEG 1, JPEG XT, JPEG XL, DASH Part 9 (REaP), PNG, SVG, TTML2, GIF, ID3, Standard MIDI Files, DNG, TIFF/EP, TIFF v6, RIFF, MPF and Exif. It also covers the Open Font Format and OpenType, Ogg Vorbis, ISO 28500:2017, WebVTT, CMAF, W3C XML Signature, ONNX, SafeTensors, Protocol Buffers (proto3), Enhanced RTMP (V2) and Adobe's Real Time Messaging Protocol.

Lists other normative references, including XMP and its JSON-LD serialization, the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1, Exif metadata for XMP, URNs, UUIDs, ISO 8601, RFC 3339, RFC 7826, RFC 9110, RFC 9580, Media Fragments and the Web Annotation Data Model. It also lists Brotli, Unicode Normalization Forms (UAX #15) and variation selectors, RFC 5646 (BCP 47), Atom (RFC 4287), RSS 2.0, ISO 14064-1:2018, ISO/IEC TR 20226:2025, and Subresource Integrity Level 2.

Presents Figure 4, the C2PA Entity Diagram, showing how the parts of the C2PA system integrate and relate to each other. It explains that an asset embeds a C2PA Manifest Store holding one or more C2PA Manifests, the last of which is the active manifest whose content bindings are validated against the asset's digital content. Within each manifest, the assertion store collects the assertions (including any ingredient assertions and the content binding), and the claim references them by URI and is cryptographically signed by the claim signature. Green lines in the diagram denote containment and blue lines denote logical references, and the Manifests, Assertions, Claims and Binding to Content sections give the full structural descriptions.
Heading that opens section 8 Assertions; it carries no text of its own.

Describes the expectation that each claim generator creates or assembles one or more assertions about when, where and how an asset was originated or transformed, and defines an assertion as labelled data, typically but not necessarily in a CBOR-based structure, representing a declaration about an asset. Notes that some assertions contain human-generated information and others machine-generated information, with examples including metadata, actions performed on the asset, thumbnails of the asset or its ingredients, and content bindings. States that assertions may be redacted by subsequent claims (Section 8.8 Redaction of Assertions) but cannot be modified once made as part of a claim.
Heading that opens section 8.2 Labels; it carries no text of its own.

Specifies that string values in C2PA data structures may be organized into namespaces using a period as a separator, that any string value defined in the specification shall begin with the c2pa namespace, and that the C2PA namespace registry lists other top-level namespaces. Requires entity-specific namespaces (any other than c2pa or registered ones) to begin with the entity's Internet domain name starting with a valid IANA top-level domain, similar to Java packages (e.g. com.litware), so that labels defined by different entities do not collide. Requires the period-separated components of an entity-specific namespace to follow the POSIX or C locale variable naming convention [a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*, and gives an ABNF for namespaces.

Describes assertion labels as namespaced strings defined by the C2PA specifications or an external entity, most commonly in the c2pa namespace, and versioned with a simple incrementing integer such as c2pa.actions.v2, where a missing version is considered v1. Points to Chapter 16 C2PA Standard Assertions for publicly known labels, and notes that namespacing for well-established standards is now done through entity-specific namespaces such as org.iso and org.w3. Gives an ABNF for assertion labels and states that label components follow the POSIX or C locale variable naming convention [a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*, with a repeated underscore (__) reserved for labelling multiple assertions of the same type.

Recommends that changes to an assertion's schema be backwards compatible, so new fields may be added and existing ones marked deprecated (read but never written), while existing fields shall not be removed and the label takes an incremented version number, e.g. moving from c2pa.actions to c2pa.actions.v2. Optional fields may be added without changing the version number. Requires deprecated fields of C2PA standard assertions to be indicated in Chapter 16 C2PA Standard Assertions and forbids claim generators from inserting data into deprecated fields. Requires a non-backwards-compatible change to give the assertion a new label rather than a higher version number, such as the fictional c2pa.component replacing c2pa.ingredient.

Specifies that multiple assertions of the same type in one manifest are given unique labels by appending a double underscore and a monotonically increasing index, e.g. c2pa.metadata, c2pa.metadata__1 and c2pa.metadata__2. When a label includes a version number, the instance number follows the versioned label, e.g. c2pa.ingredient.v2__2.

Recommends that claim generators use the schemas in the document and the machine-readable ones from the C2PA website to ensure their assertions are consistent with the expected structures, noting that the schemas also aid understanding of the syntax. States that validators should not validate inputs against these schemas.

Defines the assertion store as the logical collection of assertions referenced by a claim in a manifest, which shall be stored as described in Section 11.5 Serialization. Requires each assertion referenced in a claim's created_assertions or gathered_assertions (but not redacted_assertions) to be present in the assertion store of the same C2PA Manifest as the claim. Notes that each manifest has a single assertion store but an asset may have several, and recommends that each assertion include a randomly-generated salt in the private c2sh box within its JUMBF Description Box (Section 9.4.2.3 Hashing JUMBF Boxes) so subsequent generators can redact assertions securely.

Describes how assertion data that is large or infrequently needed may be hosted externally and referenced by URI instead of being embedded in the assertion store, using either a cloud data assertion for remotely stored C2PA assertions (JUMBF) or an external reference assertion for remotely stored assertion or non-assertion data. In both cases the externally hosted data is not retrieved or validated as part of manifest validation, and is only retrieved and validated when an application specifically needs it, under the rules in Section 14.10 Validate the Assertions.

Defines redaction as removing assertions from an asset-embedded manifest when the asset is used as an ingredient, and requires it to be done either by removing the entire assertion from the assertion store or by replacing its content per Section 14.10.3 Redacted Assertion Representation. Requires a URI reference to the redacted assertion in the claim's redacted_assertions field, strongly recommends a c2pa.redacted action with a redacted field, and requires an ingredient manifest to be removed from the C2PA Manifest Store when redacting its ingredient assertion leaves no other references to it; because the URI includes the assertion label, the type of removed information remains known. Recommends documenting a redaction with an update manifest unless it accompanies changes to data covered by content bindings. Forbids claim generators from redacting c2pa.actions or c2pa.actions.v2 assertions, and from redacting the hard binding assertion for the current asset when creating an update manifest; validator handling is described in Section 14.10 Validate the Assertions.

Specifies that the default date/time value in an assertion is serialized as CBOR tag 0 and represented in CDDL as tdate, which requires an explicit timezone or Z. Distinguishes the evidentiary meanings of standard time values (the signer's claim of the time), a claimed time of signing (signer-claimed and not independently authoritative), and a trusted time stamp (TSA evidence about the data submitted to it). Specifies that claim generator timestamp fields use generator-lower-bound-time-type or generator-upper-bound-time-type, taking a direct tdate or a map with a tdate in value and an optional timeStampType, and that a value without timeStampType shall be interpreted as absolute; lowerBound and upperBound give bounds without guaranteeing the actual time and, on start and end fields, bracket when the process or action occurred. Notes that the claimed time of signing uses CBOR tag 1 (seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00Z), that the time stamp assertion uses standard time-stamping formats, and that the different representations allow the most appropriate standards-based form for each use case.
Heading that opens section 9 Unique Identifiers; it carries no text of its own.

Specifies that every C2PA Manifest is uniquely identified by a URN from the c2pa URN namespace and that a C2PA asset is identified by the c2pa URN of its active manifest. The URN consists of the required urn:c2pa identifier and UUID v4 string, optionally followed by a Claim Generator identifier (no more than 32 ASCII characters that are not control or graphic characters) and a Version and Reason string (a positive integer, an underscore and another positive integer), separated by colons. When a Version and Reason string is present, a Claim Generator identifier shall also be present but may be empty; an ABNF and examples are given. Notes that earlier versions used a UUID URN with the claim generator identifier first, which did not comply with RFC 9562 or RFC 8141, and that the c2pa URN is used, for example, to identify an asset as an ingredient.

Describes situations where a C2PA Manifest must be re-labelled due to an identifier conflict, such as an ingredient manifest with the same label but different content being added to an asset's C2PA Manifest Store, and requires the modified copy to be re-labelled. To re-label, the claim generator shall append a colon if the URN has no Claim Generator identifier string and then, in all cases, append a colon followed by a monotonically increasing integer starting at 1, an underscore, and a reason code, where 1 means conflict with another C2PA Manifest. For example, a second re-labelling due to conflict appends :2_1.

Requires that, for assets without a C2PA Manifest but with embedded XMP containing xmpMM:DocumentID and/or xmpMM:InstanceID, those values be used as the asset's identifiers. For assets with neither a C2PA Manifest nor embedded XMP, the claim generator may use any method of its choosing to obtain a unique identifier.
Heading that opens section 9.4 URI References; it carries no text of its own.

Requires all references to information in the manifest, whether embedded or stored externally, to use JUMBF URI references as defined in ISO 19566-5:2023, C.2, normally within a hashed_uri or hashed_ext_uri structure, and notes that the field-referencing extension in Section 16.4.1.4.6 Unique Identifiers for Actions applies only in that context. For a compressed manifest, the URI shall be formed as if the manifest were not compressed, including the label of the c2ma or c2um box but not the c2cm box, and shall not include the label of the brob box. A validator shall treat an internal JUMBF URI reference as unresolved if any label in its path is ambiguous because multiple child boxes share that label.
Heading that opens section 9.4.2 Hashed URIs; it carries no text of its own.

Specifies that a hashed_uri is used when the URI refers to something embedded in the same C2PA Manifest Store, and gives the CDDL hashed-uri-map with a url (JUMBF URI), an optional alg, and a hash byte string. If alg is absent the algorithm is taken from an enclosing structure, the field in this structure is used if both are present, and the structure is invalid if neither supplies one. Because assertion stores shall be in the same C2PA Manifest box as the claim, only self#jumbf URIs are permitted; these may be relative to the entire C2PA Manifest Store (starting with a slash) or to the current manifest, and shall not contain the two-period sequence (..). Examples of both URI forms are given.

Specifies the hashed-ext-uri-map structure for referencing resources external to the C2PA Manifest Store, a variation of hashed-uri with an http/https url, a mandatory alg, a hash, and optional dc:format, size and data_types fields. Recommends the https scheme to protect privacy in transit but also permits http because data integrity is protected by the hash field, leaving manifest authors to choose. When present, dc:format provides an alternative to the Content-Type header and shall be used as the required format during content negotiation, and data_types may give one or more asset types for more clarity. The optional size field gives the size of the data to be retrieved and may serve validators as a hint alongside the hash, for example about whether to download, validate or both.

Requires the hash for a URI reference to any JUMBF box, such as assertions and data boxes, to be computed over the contents of the structure's JUMBF superbox, including the JUMBF Description Box and all content boxes but not the superbox header (with more detail in Section 12.1 Hashing). Defines the C2PA salt as a Private field of a JUMBF Description box whose value is a standard box with a 4-byte big-endian length, a box type of c2sh, and a payload of 16 or 32 bytes of randomly generated data. Figure 5 shows an example c2pa.actions assertion.
Heading that opens section 10 Claims; it carries no text of its own.

Defines a claim as gathering all the assertions about an asset at a given time, including those for binding to content, which is then cryptographically hashed and signed as described in Section 10.3.2.4 Signing a Claim. Specifies that a claim is encoded as a JUMBF superbox labelled c2pa.claim.v2 with a CBOR payload that shall comply with the CBOR Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements. Notes that assertion metadata on claims is deprecated, and that the earlier c2pa.claim label and claim-map are deprecated: validators should still accept them, but claim generators shall not produce them.
Heading that opens section 10.2 Syntax; it carries no text of its own.

Gives the CDDL schema for claims: claim-map-v2 for the c2pa.claim.v2 label and the deprecated claim-map for c2pa.claim, with the complete normative schema in Section G.2.1 Claim. claim-map-v2 requires instanceID, claim_generator_info, signature and created_assertions, and optionally allows gathered_assertions, dc:title, redacted_assertions, alg, alg_soft, and the deprecated specVersion and metadata fields; the deprecated claim-map instead carries claim_generator, a claim_generator_info array, an assertions list and dc:format. It also defines generator-info-map with a required name and optional version, icon, operating_system, specVersion and any additional fields. An example claim-map-v2 is given in CBOR diagnostic notation.

Specifies the claim's fields. The alg field, if present, shall be an allowed hash algorithm from Section 12.1 Hashing and applies to any hashed-uri, hard binding assertion or hash assertion that does not define its own, and if alg is absent each of those shall declare its algorithm explicitly. dc:title, if present, shall be a human-readable name for the asset, though claim generators should instead create a metadata assertion with dc:title; instanceID should be the asset's xmpMM:InstanceID when XMP is present, and otherwise some other unique identifier shall be used. The signature field shall be present with an absolute URI reference to the claim signature in the same C2PA Manifest, and created_assertions shall be present with one or more references to assertions made by the claim, attributed to the signer and including at least a hard binding assertion in a standard manifest. When present, gathered_assertions references assertions provided by other workflow components that are not attributed to the signer, and redacted_assertions references redacted assertions; the notes add that dc:format is no longer in c2pa.claim.v2, that XMP-derived field names do not require XMP, and that the claim-level specVersion is deprecated in favour of the one in claim_generator_info.
Heading that opens section 10.2.3 Claim Generator Info; it carries no text of its own.

Requires detailed information about the claim generator to be present as the value of claim_generator_info, and requires a Manifest Consumer to use that value to determine information about the claim generator for itself or for presentation in a UX. Notes that the simple-string claim_generator field of c2pa.claim is no longer present in c2pa.claim.v2.

Specifies that a claim_generator_info value is a generator-info-map that shall contain a name field and may contain version, icon, or both, plus any other fields using entity-specific namespacing, and that it shall represent the non-human (hardware or software) actor that generated the claim. If present, icon shall be a hashed URI to an embedded data assertion labelled c2pa.icon that follows the multiple-instance label rules, with its hash algorithm taken from the hashed URI's alg or else the claim's alg, and Manifest Consumers should also support the data box approach of earlier versions. A specVersion field should be present and, if so, shall contain the SemVer version of the specification the claim generator used to create the manifest (e.g. 2.4.0), which validators should treat as purely informational without changing their validation logic. A JSON example is included.
Heading that opens section 10.3 Creating a Claim; it carries no text of its own.

States that before a claim can be finalized, all assertions need to be created and stored in a newly created C2PA Assertion Store. When creating a standard manifest where not all binding information is known at claim creation time, it directs use of the multiple step processing method to set up the information and fill it in later.
Heading that opens section 10.3.2 Preparing the Claim; it carries no text of its own.

Requires the claim to contain a created_assertions field and allows a gathered_assertions field, whose combined values list the URI references of all assertions added to the assertion store that the claim is claiming. In a standard manifest, created_assertions shall include at least one assertion representing a hard binding. URI references to any assertions in ingredient claims that are being redacted shall be added to the redacted_assertions field.

Describes ingredients as existing assets an actor brings in to create a derived asset, composed asset or asset rendition, documented in the provenance data through ingredient assertions. Recommends inserting an ingredient's C2PA Manifests into the asset's C2PA Manifest Store, as described in Section 11.4 Ingredient Storage. If a manifest with the same unique identifier is already present, the two shall be compared: an identical new manifest shall be ignored, while a different one shall be added after its identifier is changed per Chapter 9 Unique Identifiers. If an ingredient's remote manifest cannot be retrieved, the claim generator should use the error code manifest.inaccessible.

Explains that although the signature cannot be part of the signed payload, its label is predefined, so its full URI reference is known and is set as the value of the claim's signature field. This provides the explicit binding of the claim to its signature.

Refers to Section 12.3 Digital Signatures for producing the signature, and requires that for both standard and update manifests the payload field of Sig_structure be the serialized CBOR of the claim document, using detached content mode. The resulting serialized COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure is written into the C2PA Claim Signature box.
Heading that opens section 10.3.2.5 Time Stamps; it carries no text of its own.

Recommends that, if possible, the claim generator use an RFC 3161-compliant Time Stamping Authority to obtain a trusted time stamp proving the signature existed at a certain date and time, incorporated into the COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure as a countersignature. Encourages including time stamps because, per Chapter 14 Validation, manifests without them cease to be valid when the signing credential expires or is revoked. Requires a manifest to contain only one time stamp, noting that earlier versions allowed multiple.

Defines the deprecated v1 payload (in a v1 time stamp) as the same payload value used in the Sig_signature for signing the claim, which a claim generator shall not create but a validator shall process if present. Defines the v2 payload (in a v2 time stamp) as the value of the signature field of the COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure created when signing the claim, including the entire serialized bstr with its major type and length bytes, and requires claim generators to use it when time stamping.

Requires all time stamps to be obtained per RFC 3161 with additional requirements. The MessageImprint of the TimeStampReq shall be computed from the RFC 9052 ToBeSigned value, using a Sig_structure whose context is CounterSignature, whose payload is as described in Section 10.3.2.5.2 Choosing the Payload, and whose other elements follow Section 12.3.3 Computing the Signature. The ToBeSigned value is hashed with an algorithm from the allowed list in Section 12.1 Hashing that the TSA supports (a TSA supporting none cannot be used), preferably the same algorithm as the claim's digital signature. The certReq boolean shall be asserted so that the TSA's certificate chain is provided in the response.

Specifies that deprecated v1 time stamps are stored in a COSE unprotected header labelled sigTst whose value shall be a tstContainer, with the content of the TSA's TimeStampResp stored as the val of a tstTokens element. v2 time stamps shall be stored in a COSE unprotected header labelled sigTst2 as a tstContainer, with the timeStampToken from the TimeStampResp stored as val and formatted as a DER-encoded RFC 3161 TimeStampToken in a CBOR byte string; a note equates this to the CTT model of the IETF COSE time-stamp header draft, serving as a countersignature over the complete signature structure. If no time stamps are included, neither sigTst nor sigTst2 shall be present. The tstContainer CDDL is given and noted to be a CBOR adaptation of a subset of the JAdES schema, with val as a byte string rather than Base64.

Recommends that if the signer's credential supports online credential status queries and points to a service providing status information with a time stamp, the claim generator query it, capture the response, and store it as described for credentials in the Trust Model. If credential revocation information is attached this way, a trusted time stamp shall also be obtained after signing, as described in Section 10.3.2.5 Time Stamps.
Heading that opens section 10.3.3 Examples of Claims; it carries no text of its own.
Presents Figure 6, a visual representation of an image with a single embedded claim containing multiple assertions.
Presents Figure 7, showing a second claim created for the single-claim example in which one of the original assertions has been redacted from the previous claim.
Heading that opens section 11 Manifests; it carries no text of its own.

Describes a C2PA Manifest as a container bundling an assertion store, a claim that hashes the assertions and provides information about the claim generator, and a claim signature over that claim. The manifest that describes the asset is the active manifest, and because ingredients may have their own manifests, all manifests associated with an asset are collected into a single C2PA Manifest Store. A standard C2PA Manifest includes a hard binding cryptographically associating it with the asset, so copying or linking it to a different asset is detectable and fails validation; serialization details are in Section 11.5 Serialization.

Defines a C2PA Manifest Store as containing one or more C2PA Manifests, the last of which is the active manifest, and specifies that it is a JUMBF (ISO 19566-5:2023) superbox, with details in Section 11.5 Serialization. Figure 8 shows an example store with a single C2PA Manifest.
Heading that opens section 11.3 Types of Manifests; it carries no text of its own.
Requires every C2PA Manifest to contain an assertion store, a claim and a claim signature.
Requires a standard C2PA Manifest to contain exactly one hard binding to content assertion.

Recommends an Update Manifest when assertions are added to an existing C2PA Manifest without changing the digital content or other data covered by content bindings, and forbids it from containing c2pa.hash.data, c2pa.hash.boxes, c2pa.hash.collection.data, c2pa.hash.segment, c2pa.hash.bmff.v3 or c2pa.hash.multi-asset assertions. Where the existing content binding locates the C2PA Manifest Store by file offset and length, the store shall start at the same offset after updating, though its length may change. An Update Manifest may contain c2pa.actions or c2pa.actions.v2 assertions only with the actions c2pa.edited.metadata, c2pa.opened, c2pa.published or c2pa.redacted, and shall not contain a thumbnail assertion, since other actions or a thumbnail imply changes to the digital content. It shall contain exactly one c2pa.ingredient.v3 assertion with activeManifest and claimSignature URI references to the updated asset's C2PA Manifest and Claim Signature and a relationship of parentOf, where that ingredient manifest may be a standard or update manifest.

Describes how, when a C2PA Manifest includes ingredient assertions and an ingredient contains a C2PA Manifest Store, its C2PA Manifests are normally included in the new asset's C2PA Manifest Store to keep the provenance data intact, as described in Section 10.3.2.2 Adding Ingredients. Figure 9 shows a C2PA Manifest Store with an ingredient. Notes that the previously supported Data Box Store (c2pa.databoxes) is covered for historical reference in Section H.4 Data Box Store of Appendix H Deprecated Constructs.

Specifies that C2PA Manifest Stores and C2PA Manifests are serialized using JUMBF (ISO 19566-5:2023), and that this format shall also be used in formats without native JUMBF support or when stores are kept separately from the asset. Table 2 gives the JUMBF type UUID, label and contents for the Manifest Store (c2pa), standard manifest (c2ma), update manifest (c2um), compressed manifest (c2cm), deprecated standard manifest type (c2md), Assertion Store (c2as, label c2pa.assertions), Claim (c2cl, label c2pa.claim.v2) and Claim Signature (c2cs, label c2pa.signature). These boxes shall satisfy Section 11.5.3.2 Toggles and Section 11.5.3.3 Labels, and Manifest Consumers shall accept c2md superboxes as standard manifests while claim generators shall not create them.

Specifies that the C2PA Assertion Store is a JUMBF superbox with the label and type given in Table 2, containing one or more C2PA Assertion superboxes whose JUMBF type defines the type of their content sub-boxes. Each assertion superbox shall have a label as defined in Standard Assertions and contain a JUMBF Description Box, one or more JUMBF Content Boxes and possibly a Padding Box. Recommends CBOR, JSON, Embedded File (bfdb and bidb) or UUID content types while permitting any JUMBF content type and a JUMBF Protection Box per ISO 19566-4:2020, and notes that custom formats such as encrypted data are supported through a UUID Content Box.

Specifies that standard and update C2PA Manifests can be compressed in their entirety using a new brob JUMBF content box with box ID 0x62726F62, based on a similar JPEG-XL box. A compressed manifest shall have a TYPE of c2cm, a label identical to that of the compressed manifest superbox, and brob contents that are the Brotli-compressed (RFC 7932) bytes of the entire manifest superbox, as shown in Figure 10. Hashing a compressed box follows Section 9.4.2.3 Hashing JUMBF Boxes, covering the Description Box and the brob box with its compressed payload without decompressing it first. Anywhere the specification references a standard or update manifest, a compressed one is also valid.
Heading that opens section 11.5.3 General C2PA JUMBF Requirements; it carries no text of its own.

Requires that a C2PA Manifest Consumer never process an assertion, assertion store, claim, claim signature or C2PA Manifest that is not contained in a C2PA Manifest Store, and that it skip over and ignore the contents of any JUMBF box or superbox whose type UUID it does not recognize. Notes that this lets a consumer process private boxes it knows about while ignoring unknown ones.

Requires the Label Present toggle (xxxxxx1x) and the Requestable toggle (xxxxxx11) to be set on all JUMBF Description boxes used in a C2PA Manifest, because labels are required and boxes are referred to by JUMBF URIs. When a salt is included in a PRIVATE box as described in Section 9.4.2.3 Hashing JUMBF Boxes, the Private toggle (xxx1xxxx) shall also be set.

Requires JUMBF labels to be stored as null-terminated Unicode characters in UTF-8, per ISO 19566-5:2023, A.3. Labels may not contain characters in the ranges U+0000 to U+001F or U+007F to U+009F, or the characters '/', ';', '?' and '#', and because labels are used in JUMBF URIs, U+FEFF, U+FFFF and U+D800-U+DFFF shall also not be used.

Allows the C2PA Manifest Store (c2pa) and C2PA Manifests (c2ma, c2um, c2cm and c2md) to contain JUMBF boxes and superboxes whose type UUIDs are not defined in the specification, provided they satisfy Section 11.5.3.2 Toggles and Section 11.5.3.3 Labels, enabling custom extensions and future additions without breaking compatibility. Requires any box or superbox with both the Requestable and Label Present toggles set to be maintained in any updated C2PA Manifest Store, since such boxes are intended to be referenced via JUMBF URIs and removing them could cause downstream workflows to fail.

Explains why JUMBF (ISO 19566-5:2023) was chosen to serialize C2PA Manifests: it can store multiple manifests in one container, refer to elements within and across manifests via URIs, clearly identify the parts of an element to be hashed, and store both C2PA's predefined data types (e.g. JSON and CBOR) and arbitrary data formats. It is also natively supported by the JPEG family and compatible with the ISO BMFF box model, letting it work with classic image formats such as JPEG/JFIF and PNG as well as 3D and document formats such as PDF. A note explains that using CBOR for the entire manifest was considered but not chosen because CBOR is not a container format, and re-implementing JUMBF's features in CBOR would be a lot of work and would not fully remove the need for a JUMBF/BMFF parser.

States that a C2PA Manifest Store can be embedded into a variety of file formats covering images, video, audio, fonts and documents, with technical details for each supported format in Appendix A Embedding manifests. Notes that many classic image formats such as BMP do not support embedding arbitrary data, so an external manifest is required for them.

Explains that some file formats require the file offsets of the C2PA Manifest Store and asset content to be fixed before signing so content bindings align, yet the size of the manifest and its signature cannot be precisely known until after signing, citing JPEG 1, where the entire Manifest Store must appear before the image data. Requires a multiple step approach, similar to how PDF signatures are done, to accomplish this.

Requires a standard manifest's claim to include one or more content binding assertions so that the asset is tamper-evident, and describes creating the data hash assertion using exclusion ranges, where a single hash covers only the asset ranges outside the exclusions (e.g. the claim creator may exclude the APP11 segments holding a manifest in a JPEG 1 file). To prevent insertion attacks a single exclusion range is desirable; when the manifest's size or location is unknown, start and length shall both be zero and pad should be large enough for the values written in the second pass, with at least 16 bytes recommended and pad consisting of all 0x00 bytes. Claim generators shall ensure that changes to pad data or other excluded data cannot change how the asset is interpreted; for JPEG 1, a note says this can be achieved by eliminating padding or by including all APP11 segment headers and 2-byte length fields in the data-hash-map.

Describes adding the data hash assertion reference to the claim's assertion list with a temporary hash value, such as empty spaces, after which the temporary claim can be added to the C2PA Manifest. Because the temporary claim cannot be signed yet, it describes building a temporary COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure so the claim signature box holds valid CBOR. The four-element array consists of an empty protected header bucket (a zero-length bstr), an unprotected header map with one pad entry holding a zero-filled bstr of the desired padding size (25 kilobytes is recommended initially), a nil payload, and a zero-length bstr signature.

Describes completing the C2PA Manifest by assembling all its boxes into final form and combining the asset's manifest with the manifests of any ingredients into the complete C2PA Manifest Store. Requires the active manifest to be the last C2PA Manifest superbox in the C2PA Manifest Store superbox, after which the store can be embedded into the asset as discussed in Appendix A, Embedding manifests.

Describes updating the data hash assertion with the active manifest's starting offset and length after embedding, without changing the assertion box's size, by adjusting the pad field; a note explains that some padding sizes cannot be expressed in pad alone and can be split between pad and pad2. The updated assertion is then hashed into the reserved space, and the claim is hashed and signed per Section 10.3.2.4, Signing a Claim, with the unprotected pad header shrunk so the claim signature box keeps its size. Requires repeating the multiple step processing with larger padding chosen in Section 11.7.2 if the serialized COSE_Sign1_Tagged exceeds the reserved size, noting that still-valid revocation information should be reusable but a new time stamp will be required. Recommends that claim generators use padding before assertion creation when assertions defined outside this specification may depend on file layout.

Describes keeping C2PA Manifests external to the asset, in a manifest repository easily locatable by a Manifest Consumer (such as by reference or URI), when embedding is not possible or practical. Requires the C2PA Manifest Store to be served with the media type application/c2pa, noting that application/x-c2pa-manifest-store is deprecated. Lists common reasons for external manifests: embedding may be technically impossible, impractical when the manifest store is larger than the asset's digital content, or inappropriate when the asset cannot be modified.

Recommends that, when an asset has embedded XMP and its C2PA Manifest Store is stored externally, the claim generator add a dcterms:provenance key to the XMP whose value is a URI reference to the manifest store. Notes that this mechanism is now only for external manifests, and that fonts, which do not support XMP, use an equivalent method described in the clause on fonts.
Heading that opens Chapter 12, Cryptography; it carries no text of its own.

Requires all cryptographic hashes used in creating and validating C2PA Manifests to use algorithms from an allowed list (generators should use, validators shall support) or a deprecated list (validators should support, generators shall not produce), excluding soft bindings and custom assertions. Requires that an algorithm appear in at most one list, that each output length be listed separately, and that unlisted algorithms be forbidden and not supported optionally. Requires hash outputs to be stored as CBOR byte strings with an algorithm identifier (alg) in the same structure, an enclosing structure, or the claim-map or claim-map-v2, with the nearest identifier taking precedence and the claim-map alg used as the fallback. The allowed list is SHA2-256 (sha256), SHA2-384 (sha384) and SHA2-512 (sha512); SHA-3 is excluded for consistency with the signature algorithm list, and the deprecated list is empty.
Heading that opens section 12.2 Binding to Content; it carries no text of its own.

Describes content bindings in a standard C2PA manifest, distinguishing hard (cryptographic) bindings, which let a validator confirm the manifest belongs to this asset and that the asset is unmodified, from soft bindings, which are computed from the digital content and help identify derived assets and renditions. Requires that a single manifest contain no more than one hard binding assertion, while allowing zero or more soft binding assertions.

States that every hard binding assertion is built from the hash algorithms defined in Section 12.1, Hashing, and that the specific hard binding assertion used depends on the asset's format and structure, as described in the following subsections.

Describes the simplest hard binding as a cryptographic hash over some or all bytes of an asset, usable on any asset type but recommended only for formats that do not support box-based hashing. Specifies that a data hash assertion defines which byte ranges are hashed, works for single binaries or multi-chunk assets, and binds a C2PA Manifest to the codec configuration of live media over Enhanced RTMP (V2), as described in Section 15.5.3.3, Initialization data binding.

Recommends using a general box hash assertion for non-BMFF box-based formats such as JPEG 1, PNG and GIF. Describes the assertion as an array of structures, each listing one or more boxes by name or identifier with a hash covering those boxes (and any data between them) and the hashing algorithm used.

Permits ISO BMFF-based assets to use BMFF-based hash assertions instead, which for a monolithic MP4 with mdat validated as a unit work nearly like a data hash assertion but use a box exclusion list rather than byte ranges. Requires that, for fragmented MP4 files, the assertion be combined with chunk-specific hashing information located as specified in Section A.5, Embedding manifests into BMFF-based assets, and points to the live media section for hashing individual segments.

Requires a data hash assertion for unstructured text assets whose C2PA Manifest is embedded using Unicode Variation Selectors as described in Section A.8, Embedding Manifests into Unstructured Text. The hashing follows the text-specific normalization rules defined in Validating a text data hash.

Requires a data hash assertion for structured text assets associated with a C2PA Manifest using ASCII armour-style delimiters as described in Section A.9, Embedding Manifests into Structured Text. The exclusion range covers the manifest block so the hash is computed without the manifest reference, with details in Section A.9.5, Hard Binding.

Requires a segment hash assertion for files written only by appending complete lines, such as application logs, event logs and JSON Lines streams, as described in Section A.3.17, Embedding manifests into append-only text files. Each assertion is a hard binding over one bounded segment, and the segments are linked into a chain of checkpoints so the file's complete history can be verified.

Requires the collection data hash assertion to be used to specify hard bindings when a C2PA Manifest refers to a collection of assets rather than a single asset. A note gives the example of describing each folder of an AI/ML training data set.

Requires the multi-asset hash assertion, alongside the whole-file hard binding assertion, for formats that aggregate multiple independently verifiable parts, such as CIPA Multi-Picture Format (MPF) or Android Ultra HDR, recording a hash for each part. States that a multi-asset hash assertion modifies how a hard binding is validated but is not itself a hard binding.

Recommends that a Claim Generator, where possible, include asset metadata outside the C2PA Manifest, such as EXIF or XMP, in the hard binding to protect its integrity. A note clarifies that only signed C2PA created_assertions are attributed to the signer, so metadata covered only by a hard binding is not, whereas serializing it into a c2pa.metadata assertion in created_assertions explicitly signals that the signer asserts it. Recommends copying asset metadata values supported by the common metadata assertion, as described in Appendix C, into such an assertion when the signer can assert them.
Heading that opens section 12.2.3 Soft Bindings; it carries no text of its own.

Describes soft bindings, expressed through soft binding assertions such as a fingerprint of the digital content or an invisible watermark, as enabling digital content to be matched even when the underlying bits differ, for example in another resolution or encoding. Notes that if a manifest is removed from an asset but a copy remains in a provenance store, soft bindings may be used to match the two. Requires that a soft binding not be used as a hard binding.

Specifies that soft bindings are generated by an algorithm named in the alg field of the soft binding assertion, and recommends that the name be among those in the soft binding algorithm list supported by this specification.

Requires all claim signatures to use digital signature algorithms and key types from an allowed list (generators should use, validators shall support) or a deprecated list (validators should support, generators shall not use), excluding custom assertions and time stamps. Specifies that the lists reference COSE algorithm identifiers from standards such as RFC 9052, RFC 9053, RFC 8230 and RFC 9964, which also specify the hash used in each signature scheme. Requires that Section 12.1, Hashing, not apply to those hash algorithms, whose use is allowed and followed for any listed signature algorithm.

Lists the allowed claim signature algorithms: ES256, ES384, ES512, ESP256, ESP384, ESP512, PS256, PS384, PS512, EdDSA (Ed25519 only), and ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 (COSE identifiers -48, -49, -50); the deprecated list is empty. Notes cover ML-DSA's larger signature and key sizes, the fully-specified ESP identifiers binding each hash to one curve, and that certificate signing algorithms are governed separately by Section 13.5.1.1, General Requirements. Requires implementations to check that keys are correct for the chosen algorithm (P-256/P-384/P-521 curves paired with the matching ECDSA algorithms, edwards25519 for Ed25519, RSA moduli of at least 2048 bits, and ML-DSA parameter sets matching the identifier) and to refuse incorrect keys, while allowing refusal of RSA keys over 16384 bits. Recommends deterministic signature algorithms for live media streaming so segment caching is not harmed.

Specifies that the CBOR-encoded claim is signed using COSE as described in RFC 9052, sections 4.2 and 4.4, noting that payloads may be embedded or detached, in which case the COSE_Sign1_Tagged payload field is nil. Requires that the payload field of the in-memory Sig_structure always be populated with the relevant external data and never be nil. For standard or update manifests, that payload is the contents of the claim JUMBF box, as described in Section 10.3.2.4, Signing a Claim, and Section 11.5, Serialization.

Specifies additional requirements for building Sig_structure under RFC 9052, section 4.4: the context shall be Signature1 (or CounterSignature where specified, never Signature), external_aad shall be a zero-length bstr, the payload is set by each use, and the alg header shall be in body_protected. Requires all C2PA digital signatures to be COSE_Sign1_Tagged structures with the same alg header in the protected bucket. Requires a detached payload to be nil and an embedded payload to be stored as a bstr, noting that a zero-length byte array cannot indicate detached content.

Permits a claim generator to add an iat protected header with a NumericDate value as a claimed time of signing, which, if present, shall represent when the signature was generated. Notes that NumericDate is a CBOR numeric date without the leading tag 1, and that the recommendation is based on in-process JAdES updates for a generator-provided timestamp useful when no trusted time source is available but not used for certificate validity checking.

Recommends that a claim generator able to act as a validator check that its signing credential is acceptable under Chapter 13, Trust Model, and warn if it is not. Permits signing with that credential anyway, for instance when the local validator's configuration differs from that of validators used by the asset's expected audience.

Describes building an in-memory Sig_structure when verifying a signature, with body_protected filled from the COSE_Sign1_Tagged protected header bucket and the payload taken from the COSE_Sign1_Tagged payload field when present. Requires that, when the payload is detached (nil), the Sig_structure payload be populated from the same external source used when generating the signature, as defined where each signature is used.

Requires a C2PA Manifest Consumer that wants to display a signer icon or logo to look for a logotype, as defined in RFC 9399, inside the embedded certificate. If none is present, the consumer may use icons or logos from other sources in an implementation-dependent manner.
Heading that opens Chapter 13, Trust Model, with a note that "user" in this chapter refers to human actors using C2PA-compliant validators in consumption and authoring scenarios.

Presents Figure 11, the C2PA Trust Model Diagram, showing the three entities specified in the trust model, which concerns trust in a signer's identity. Describes the consumer, who is not specified in the trust model, as using the signer's identity along with other trust signals to decide whether assertions about an asset are true.

Defines identity in the trust model as the means of associating a signing key (credential) with the signer for trust decisions about anything signed with that key. Requires the credential to be listed in the COSE protected headers of the COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure, with exactly one credential across protected and unprotected headers, and requires rejecting structures with none or with two or more, including repeats of the same credential. An exception treats the same X.509 chain under both the x5chain string label and integer label 33 as a single credential, with further details in Section 13.5, X.509 Certificates.
Heading that opens section 13.3 Validation states; it carries no text of its own.

Describes a validator as a Manifest Consumer that makes validation statements about an asset and its active manifest, following the process in the validation section. The actor consuming the asset, usually through a user agent, then interprets those statements and the asset's contents to reach their own conclusions about its provenance.
Lists the states a C2PA Manifest may have based on validation statements: Well-Formed, Valid and Trusted. Notes that any Trusted manifest is also Valid, and any Valid manifest is also Well-Formed.

Defines a Valid asset as one whose content-binding-covered portions a validator reports as unmodified since the active manifest was produced (per Section 14.12, Validate the Asset's Content) and whose active manifest is Valid or Trusted.

Defines a Well-Formed C2PA Manifest as one where validation determines that its contents meet the normative requirements checked by the validation process, only assertions allowed for its manifest type are present (Section 14.10.1), its assertions meet all assertion requirements (Section 14.10.4), and any ingredients meet all ingredient requirements (Section 14.11).

Defines a Valid C2PA Manifest as one that is Well-Formed, unmodified since signing, has a claim signature with success code claimSignature.validated, receives claimSignature.insideValidity for the signature validity period, and whose signer credential is not rejected with signingCredential.ocsp.revoked. States that a Valid manifest's claim can be attributed to the claim generator identified by the claim's claim_generator_info field.
Defines a Trusted C2PA Manifest as one that is Valid and whose signing credential receives the success code signingCredential.trusted under Section 14.7, Validate the Signature.
Heading that opens section 13.4 Trust Lists; it carries no text of its own.

Requires a validator to maintain a list of accepted Extended Key Usage (EKU) values and, for each, a list of trust anchor configurations, each including the trust anchor's X.509 certificate and recommended to include notBefore and (when trust has ended) notAfter date/times. Requires that a configuration not be used for claim signatures whose timestamp, or the current time if none, falls before notBefore or after notAfter. Requires the list for the c2pa-kp-claimSigning EKU to include the C2PA Trust List, and recommends letting users configure additional anchors for that or other EKUs and offering default or externally maintained lists. Notes that including id-kp-emailProtection or id-kp-documentSigning alongside c2pa-kp-claimSigning can improve compatibility with older validators.

Requires a validator to maintain trust anchor configurations for Time Stamping Authorities (TSAs) separately from the C2PA signer lists, each including the X.509 certificate and recommended to include notBefore and notAfter date/times. Requires that a configuration not be used for time-stamps asserting times outside those bounds, and that the list include the C2PA TSA Trust List. Recommends allowing users to configure additional TSA trust anchor stores, and permits offering default or externally maintained lists.

Permits a validator to let users maintain a private credential store, an address book of signing credentials trusted through out-of-band relationships. Requires that the store apply only to validating signed C2PA manifests (not time stamps), trust only signer credentials directly, and never act as trust anchors. Requires that the store not be pre-configured and that entries be added or removed only at the user's request.

Specifies that X.509 certificates are stored per RFC 9360, quoting its x5chain definition, and adds requirements beyond it. Requires claim generators to include the signer's certificate and all intermediate CA certificates in x5chain, recommends omitting the root certificate, and notes that the first certificate's public key validates the signature. Requires claim generators to use only integer label 33 (the string label x5chain is deprecated) and to place the header only in the protected bucket. Requires validators to accept either label from either bucket, treat both labels together as one credential using label 33, and reject the signature as malformed if the same label appears in both buckets.
Heading that opens section 13.5.1 Certificate Profiles; it carries no text of its own.

Defines requirements for an X.509 certificate to be acceptable as a C2PA claim signing credential, not applying to TSA, OCSP or CA certificates. Requires the signatureAlgorithm to be one of the listed ECDSA, RSA, RSASSA-PSS, Ed25519 or ML-DSA identifiers, with constraints on RSASSA-PSS parameters, absent parameters for ML-DSA, named curves prime256v1, secp384r1 or secp521r1 for EC keys, and RSA moduli of at least 2048 bits; a note explains that RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 is permitted for CA certificate signatures but not for C2PA claims. For all certificates outside the private credential store, requires v3, no unique IDs, correct Basic Constraints (only end entity certificates sign claims, time stamps and OCSP responses), Authority and Subject Key Identifiers as prescribed, and a Key Usage extension with digitalSignature for manifest signers. Requires a non-empty EKU extension in end entity certificates, forbidding anyExtendedKeyUsage, requiring id-kp-timeStamping or id-kp-OCSPSigning for those purposes exclusively, and not rejecting certificates for unrelated extra EKUs.

Specifies that a signing certificate in the private credential store is accepted, while otherwise the trust chain shall be built and validated per RFC 5280, section 6, for the relevant purpose and trust anchor store, with any failure causing rejection; the private credential store is never used to build chains or validate time stamps. Requires validators to reject certificates used for purposes not authorized by their EKU, and requires claim signing certificates to have at least one EKU for which the validator has trust anchors, using only those anchors. Requires validators to verify Certificate Profile compliance (outside the private credential store), including EKU presence and authorization for no more than one of C2PA signing, time stamp signing or OCSP signing, and to ignore any EKU present on CA certificates.

Recommends that claim generators implement revocation using OCSP and OCSP stapling, and forbids them from using Certificate Revocation Lists, noting CRLs are slow to download and large. Recommends that CAs include an AuthorityInfoAccess extension, and requires that, when present, revocation information be stored in an unprotected COSE_Sign1 header labelled rVals following the given CDDL with an ocspVals array. Recommends that before signing, a claim generator query the OCSP service for the signer's certificate and any included intermediate CA certificates and store the responses in ocspVals, with validation described in Validate the Credential Revocation Information.
Heading that opens Chapter 14, Validation; it carries no text of its own.
Heading that opens section 14.1 Validation Process; it carries no text of its own.

Describes validation of a C2PA Manifest as a multi-step process covering its assertions, claim and claim signature, plus any associated hard bindings for active manifests only. Defines a validator as a hardware or software actor that implements the validation algorithms in this clause.

Lists the phases of validation, in no particular order: validating the assertions (Section 14.10), the ingredients if any (Section 14.11), the time stamp (Section 14.8), the credential revocation information (Section 14.9), the claim signature (Section 14.7), and the asset's content (Section 14.12). States that the results determine whether a manifest is Well-Formed, Valid or Trusted as described in Section 13.3, Validation states.
Presents Figure 12, Validating a Claim, as a visual representation of validating a C2PA Manifest, noting that the text is authoritative where it differs from the figure.
Heading that opens section 14.2 Returning Validation Results; it carries no text of its own.

Requires the validation algorithm to return a consolidated set of results, per the schema in Section 14.2.2, for all manifests in the asset's C2PA Manifest Store, including the active manifest and those referenced by ingredient assertions. Specifies standard success, informational and failure codes from Appendix D and permits custom codes that follow entity-specific namespace syntax. Requires a claim generator adding an ingredient to act as a validator, run the full algorithm on it, and record the results in the ingredient assertion's validationResults field. Permits results to include a SemVer specVersion and either a deprecated trustListUri or a trustListUris field identifying the trust lists used.

Defines, in CDDL, the data structures for validation results, with a complete normative schema in Section G.7.3. These include status-map (a code, at most one of url or resourceUrl, an optional explanation, and a deprecated success flag), status-codes-map with success, informational and failure arrays, and trust-list-uri-map with uri, type and optional identifier. Also defines validation-results-map with optional activeManifest, ingredientDeltas, specVersion, and either trustListUri (deprecated) or trustListUris, and ingredient-delta-validation-result-map with ingredientAssertionURI and validationDeltas.

Recommends that Manifest Consumers not display data from manifests or assets that are not Valid. Requires that, if such data is displayed anyway, the display include a warning about the lack of validity and a warning that the data shall not be attributed to the manifest's signer (or, for an ingredient manifest, to the asset's manifest's signer). A note says authoring scenarios should raise warnings more prominently.
Heading that opens section 14.4 Determining the hashing algorithm; it carries no text of its own.

Requires the alg field of a hard binding assertion, if present, to be used as its hashing algorithm, otherwise the Claim's alg field. Requires the Claim to be rejected with algorithm.unsupported if neither is present.

Requires the hash algorithm for a hashed_uri structure to be taken from its own alg field if present, otherwise from the nearest enclosing structure with an alg field, otherwise from the claim's alg field. Requires the claim to be rejected with algorithm.unsupported if no alg field is found in any of these locations.

Requires the alg field of a hashed_ext_uri structure, which encapsulates an external URI and its hash, to be used as its hashing algorithm, and requires the failure code algorithm.unsupported if it is absent. Notes that alg is mandatory in hashed_ext_uri, so no recursive lookup is needed.

Requires the determined hashing algorithm to be compared against the allowed and deprecated lists in Section 12.1, Hashing. Requires rejecting the claim with algorithm.unsupported if it is in neither list, and issuing the informational code algorithm.deprecated if it is in the deprecated list.
Heading that opens section 14.5 Locating the Active Manifest; it carries no text of its own.

Requires the last C2PA Manifest superbox in the C2PA Manifest Store superbox to be considered the active manifest, noting that locating the store may involve several locations and is a prerequisite with no validation status code of its own. Requires an asset to be treated as if no manifests were located when no store can be found, or when more than one store is found where an embedding method admits only one. Notes that implementations may surface additional information about why no manifests were located.
Heading that opens section 14.5.2 Embedded; it carries no text of its own.

Requires the validator to locate the C2PA Manifest Store embedded at the standard embedding locations, and permits checking an HTTP Link header if none is found. Requires multiple embedded stores to be considered invalid, with validation that should treat this as no manifests located and with none included in an ingredient assertion. Requires an embedded store to take precedence over a remote one indicated by a Link header. Requires rejection with manifest.inaccessible.encrypted if the store is unreadable due to encryption (excluding mechanisms such as the PDF Identity crypt filter) and with manifest.inaccessible.malformed if it is readable but cannot be interpreted as a valid store.

Describes how PDF incremental updates require support for multiple C2PA Manifest Stores, but only one per update section. Requires multiple stores in a single update section to be considered invalid (treated as if no manifests were located), while stores in earlier updates or the original PDF remain valid and are processed.

Requires the C2PA Manifest Store for HTML assets to be located using the procedure in Section A.7, Embedding Manifests into HTML. Requires the asset to be treated as if no manifests were located if the head element contains more than one C2PA manifest element, such as multiple script elements with type="application/c2pa" or both a script and a link element.

Requires locating the C2PA Manifest Store for structured text per Section A.9 by reading the file in binary mode and searching for the -----BEGIN C2PA MANIFEST----- and -----END C2PA MANIFEST----- delimiters, treating the asset as having no manifests if delimiters are missing, unpaired or there is more than one block. Requires extracting and whitespace-trimming the reference between delimiters. Specifies resolving a data: URI only if it has media type application/c2pa and base64 encoding, resolving other URIs per Section 14.5.3 (retrieval is optional; if not retrieved, no manifests are treated as located), and otherwise treating the asset as having no manifests.

Requires locating the C2PA Manifest Store for append-only plain-text files and JSONL streams per Section A.3.17 by scanning in binary mode from the end for the last complete sentinel line (a BEGIN/END C2PA CHECKPOINT line for plain text, or a JSON object with a c2pa:checkpoint member for JSONL). Requires treating the asset as having no manifests and reporting manifest.appendOnlyText.noSentinel if no such line is found or it is malformed.
